clue.text: Mathematician's rude bits?

parts.note: read as a whole, coarse pieces in a numbers person's world are the common kind of part-of-a-whole written with numerator over denominator

explanation.surface: A naughty question about what a mathematician keeps under wraps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rude' looks like a comment on manners or anatomy; in maths 'vulgar' is the everyday word for a common (as opposed to decimal) fraction, and 'bits' are fractions.
explanation.definitionFit: Common fractions such as three-quarters are called vulgar in the old sense of ordinary, and 'rude' is a jokey synonym for that adjective.

clue.text: Caller will put it in a mask

indicators.note: the clue says to put the word it in a mask, so the mask word is opened up and holds it

parts.note: a visor is a face shield or mask

explanation.surface: Someone who comes round will slip it into a disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: A caller is someone paying a visit to your house.

clue.text: Heather hears you, Albert, relating To the Tongue

parts.note: ling is the common heather plant

indicators.note: hears tells us the word you is taken as it sounds, giving its single-letter soundalike

parts.note: the word you is said aloud as the letter U
Al is the short form of the name Albert

explanation.surface: Heather overhears Albert talking about the tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: Heather and Albert look like two people; Heather is the plant LING and Albert gives AL. 'hears' turns 'you' into the letter U, which sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingual is the anatomical adjective for things of the tongue, from Latin lingua.

clue.text: Bet pound on final, it finishes last but two

parts.note: an ante is a stake put up before the cards are dealt
a pen or pound is an enclosure for animals
ultimate means final or last

explanation.surface: A punter backs the final, only for the horse to come in third from last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pound' looks like money for the bet, but it is an animal enclosure, PEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Antepenultimate means third from the end, one before the penultimate, which is itself one before the last.

clue.text: Old-timer is out of pocket

parts.note: read cryptically, an old-fashioned timepiece is something drawn out of a small waistcoat pocket on a chain, not a veteran short of money

explanation.surface: A veteran finds himself short of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of pocket' normally means having lost money, and 'old-timer' a veteran; here they describe an antique timepiece kept in a small waistcoat pocket and pulled out to read.
explanation.definitionFit: A pocket timepiece on a chain, kept in the little pocket called a fob, is a typically old-fashioned timekeeper.

clue.text: Dangerous sort of jazz guitarist

definitions.meaning: a man wielding a hatchet, a killer or menacing figure
in musicians' slang a guitar is an axe, so its player is named after the tool

explanation.surface: A jazz guitarist is described as a menacing type.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come from the axe: the chopping tool in a murderer's hand and the slang word for a guitar.

clue.text: This painter, with new lease, colour tutu?

indicators.note: new tells us the following letters are made into something fresh, a fresh arrangement of them

explanation.surface: An artist, given a fresh start, puts paint on a ballet skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges LEASE, COLOUR and TUTU together into the painter's name; the tutu nods to the cabaret dancers he painted.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was a French artist famous for his posters and paintings of Paris nightlife.

clue.text: Sketch of antiquated bar

parts.note: something out of fashion is out, no longer current
a bar is a line or stripe

explanation.surface: A drawing of an old-fashioned pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough sketch gives the general shape of something, its contour drawn without detail.

clue.text: Acknowledged old instrument in doleful setting

indicators.note: the mournful word is a setting for the instrument, so it surrounds it like a mount round a jewel

parts.note: doleful means sad
the lute is a stringed instrument of the medieval and Renaissance period

explanation.surface: Someone recognised an antique instrument played in a mournful scene.
explanation.definitionFit: To salute someone is to greet or recognise them with a formal gesture.

clue.text: Surface to demonstrate military tactics

parts.note: read plainly, this is a flat tray of shaped grit on which officers model terrain and move pieces to plan or teach a battle

explanation.surface: An officer looks for a flat place to show his battle plan.
explanation.definitionFit: Armies have long used a tray of moulded sand as a terrain model for planning and teaching manoeuvres.

clue.text: Up to the time bird left jauntily

indicators.note: left in the sense of having gone away: the bird departs from the word jauntily

parts.note: a jay is a bird of the crow family

explanation.surface: A bird had been strutting about cheerfully until a certain moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like a direction or past tense of leaving the scene; it removes the letters J, A and Y, scattered in order through JAUNTILY.
explanation.definitionFit: Until means up to a given point in time, as in waiting till noon.

clue.text: Rough, we hear, though trusty person

definitions.meaning: said aloud, rough sounds like ruff, which in bridge and whist means to play a card of the master suit when unable to follow suit
an old-fashioned term for a dependable, good-hearted fellow

explanation.surface: Someone sounds coarse but is reliable underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition works through a soundalike: 'Rough' is heard as 'ruff', the card-game verb that means the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games, ruffing and this verb both mean beating with the master suit; separately, the word was once slang for a splendid, loyal fellow.

clue.text: One dissecting a parti-ole is triumphant, finally

parts.note: an atom is a tiny particle, so a particle gives an atom
taken as written

indicators.note: finally picks the closing letter of the word triumphant

explanation.surface: A surgeon who cuts up a tiny particle ends up victorious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a particle' gives AN ATOM, so the 'a' is part of the piece, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist in bodily structure learns it by cutting up corpses, so the one doing the dissecting is this scientist.

clue.text: Roundly kiss for a type of sweater

parts.note: to roll is to turn round and round, so moving roundly is rolling
to neck is to kiss and cuddle

explanation.surface: Someone gives a hearty kiss to get hold of a jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is the British word for a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A pullover with a high collar folded over on itself is named for its turned-down collar.

clue.text: Outsize nurse in port

parts.note: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize
to tend is to nurse or look after

explanation.surface: A very large nurse is working in a harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostend is a ferry harbour on the Belgian coast.

clue.text: Unusual depicter of the incapacitated

indicators.note: unusual signals the letters of depicter being put in an out-of-the-ordinary order

explanation.surface: An odd artist who paints disabled people.
explanation.definitionFit: Decrepit means worn out and weakened by age or illness, unable to function properly.

clue.text: Keep on board

definitions.meaning: a keep is a fortified tower, the stronghold of a medieval fort
a rook, the chess piece found on the board

explanation.surface: Hold on to something on the chessboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortress is the stronghold of the first sense, and the chess rook has the same name in the second.

clue.text: Tip given to hatter?

definitions.meaning: to tip over is to overturn, as a boat does
a milliner is told the measure of a customer's head so that the headgear fits

explanation.surface: A gratuity handed to a milliner.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat that overturns tips over; the second reading splits the word into the head measurement a hat-maker needs.

clue.text: Rose failed to keep date

definitions.meaning: rose as the past tense of rise, got to one's feet
to stand someone up is to not turn up for an arranged romantic meeting

explanation.surface: Rose did not show up for her date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a girl's name; it is the verb, got up.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting to your feet and leaving a date waiting are both expressed by the same phrasal verb in its past tense.

clue.text: Workers surround bar, using direct routes

indicators.note: the workers are said to surround the bar, so their word goes round the other

parts.note: worker bees are the classic crossword workers
a bar is a line

explanation.surface: Staff crowd round the pub counter, taking the shortest paths.
explanation.definitionFit: Bees were believed to fly straight home, so a straight path takes its name from them.

clue.text: Everybody in support of potentially bent game

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece supporting another sits below it
potentially says the word bent may become something else, a different arrangement of its letters

parts.note: everybody means all

explanation.surface: Everyone backs a sport that may be corrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potentially' rearranges BENT into NETB; 'in support of' puts ALL below it, since this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Netball is a team sport played mainly by women, similar to basketball.

clue.text: Shrewdly cunning around trading-centre

indicators.note: around tells us the cunning word wraps round the trading-centre word

parts.note: sly means cunning
a mart is a market

explanation.surface: Someone acts astutely, using craft around the market.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting cleverly and with good judgement is acting astutely, in a sharp way.

clue.text: Jewel in one of twin stars

parts.note: a gem is a jewel
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A gem set in one of a pair of stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link but supplies its own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The constellation of the Twins is named after its two bright stars, Castor and Pollux.

clue.text: Fleece in fete, prior to exchange

indicators.note: to exchange is to swap things round, so the letters of the two words trade places

explanation.surface: A con at the village fair before a swap.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece is to overcharge, and to profiteer is to make excessive gains by exploiting buyers.

clue.text: Extremist in lawful trade

indicators.note: in shows the letters sit inside the run of words lawful trade

explanation.surface: A radical among people doing legitimate business.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is in lawfUL TRAde.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultra is someone holding extreme views, especially in politics.

clue.text: Fashionable to have help, when retired, in the country

parts.note: in means fashionable

indicators.note: retired as in withdrawn, going back, so the word for help is turned back to front

parts.note: aid means help

explanation.surface: Being trendy means getting help in rural parts after retiring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when retired' reverses AID to give DIA.
explanation.definitionFit: India is a country in South Asia.

clue.text: Far-reaching insect following bearing

indicators.note: following puts the insect after the other piece

parts.note: import as meaning or significance, the bearing something has
an ant is an insect

explanation.surface: A bug coming after something carried in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bearing' looks like a direction; it means significance, IMPORT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with far-reaching effects is significant, of great consequence.

clue.text: Scaly epithelium, with easier terms, stated so?

indicators.note: with easier terms suggests the letters of the medical phrase are put into a different, gentler form, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A doctor's polite phrase for flaky skin, said in kinder words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with easier terms' rearranges SCALY EPITHELIUM; the phrase itself is a genteel name for dandruff, so it is 'stated so', in a softened way.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something in a mild or indirect way to avoid offence is speaking in a softened manner.
